title: Comprehensive analysis of the clinical and biological significances of polyamine metabolism in glioma

sections.abstract:
Polyamines, including spermidine, spermine, and putrescine, are polycationic alkylamines in mammalian cells. However, the prognostic impact of polyamine in glioma remains unclear. In the present study, we performed bioinformatic analysis to characterize the expression of polyamine metabolism family members in patients with glioma. A prognostic gene model was conducted based on the 13 prognostic polyamine metabolism genes. The nomogram exhibited excellent performance in predicting the survival rates of glioma patients. Enrichment analysis showed that the characteristics of genes related to polyamine metabolism affected glioma in many ways, especially related to tumor inflammation, hypoxia and IL6/JAK/STAT3 pathway. In vitro experiments demonstrated that targeting SMS protein could effectively inhibit the proliferation and invasion of glioma cells. What’s more, IHC staining was conducted on glioma tissue microarrays to confirm the expression patterns of genes related to polyamine metabolism in glioma tissues. In summary, polyamine metabolism is a powerful prognostic indicator and can be used as a promising target to strengthen the personalized treatment of glioma.The developed system can improve our understanding of the role of polyamine metabolism in gliomas, paving the way for more precise and effective treatment strategies.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s12672-025-03126-6.
sections.introduction:
Glioma is the most common primary intracranial malignant tumor in adults [ 1 ]. The prognosis of patients with glioma is generally poor, with high recurrence and mortality rates. Gliomas are divided into grade I-IV, and grade I-III gliomas are classified as low-grade glioma (LGG) [ 2 ]. The median 5-year survival time of high-grade gliomas, such as glioblastoma (GBM), is only 15 months [ 3 ]. The new guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of gliomas do not only consider the classification, diagnosisو and prognosis of gliomas but also integrate the classification, optimization and updates of the traditional glioma morphological classification methods of the World Health Organization (WHO) [ 4 ].

This new classification method, which considers molecular typing as the core basis, not only increases the accuracy and reliability of diagnosis but also more accurately predicts the prognosis and guides treatment [ 5 ]. Despite these advances, due to the high heterogeneity of gliomas, existing classification systems cannot fully address individual differences among patients, making them unsuitable for robust risk stratification of patients with glioma [ 6 ]. Therefore, there is an urgent need to find more prognostic biomarkers and combine them with the classification of the World Health Organization to better predict prediction and determine treatment strategies.

Polyamines (PA), including spermidine, spermidine, and putrescine, are polycationic alkylamines in mammalian cells. They play an important role in cell growth and survival, maintain protein and nucleic acid synthesis, stabilize chromatin structure, induce cell apoptosis and differentiation, and protect cells from nucleic acid depurination and oxidative damage. They also regulate cellular communication through ion channels [ 7 , 8 ].

Recently, great progress has been made in elucidating the complex relationship between polyamine metabolism and tumorigenesis [ 9 , 10 ]. Abnormal polyamine metabolism is related to the development of many types of tumors [ 11 ]. In normal physiological conditions, the cellular content of polyamines is regulated by the complex mechanism of anabolism and transport. However, this balance is impaired in the tumor environment. Studies have shown that increased levels of polyamines are often observed in cancer cells, and these polyamines regulate various signaling pathways that lead to uncontrolled growth of malignant cells [ 12 ]. Enzymes involved in the biosynthesis, transport, and catabolism of polyamines are often dysregulated in cancer, which further emphasizes the importance of polyamine metabolism in tumorigenesis [ 13 , 14 ]. In addition, changes in the expression of key polyamine metabolic genes are associated with poor prognosis in some types of cancer [ 15 – 17 ].

In the present study, we performed bioinformatics analysis to characterize the expression of polyamine metabolism family members in patients with glioma. We utilized the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas (CGGA) RNA sequencing datasets to investigate the relationship between polyamine metabolism gene expression profiles and patients’ survival. We used the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) to develop 13 genetic risk characteristics. We characterized the relationship between this risk score and the clinical characteristics of patients with glioma. Polyamine metabolism prognostic signature was developed in this study. Remarkably, the nomogram exhibited excellent performance in predicting the survival rates of glioma patients. The results of immunohistochemistry indicated a strong correlation between SMS protein expression and high-grade gliomas or PD-L1 protein expression. In vitro experiments have shown that SMS knockdown can significantly inhibit the proliferation and invasion ability of glioma cells. Mechanistically, knocking down SMS inhibits phosphorylation of the IL-6-activated JAK/STAT3 pathway. The developed system can improve our understanding of the role of polyamine metabolism in gliomas, paving the way for more precise and effective treatment strategies.
sections.discussion:
Recently, accumulating evidence has shown that metabolic reprogramming is a major hallmark of malignant tumors [ 20 ]. Polyamines facilitate angiogenesis to provide nutrients for tumor cells. The MYC signaling pathway is a major driver of cancer associated with dysregulation of polyamine metabolism. As MYC family members are frequently amplified or overexpressed in cancer, regulation of polyamine biosynthesis by MYC family genes plays an important role in multiple cancer types [ 21 ]. Recently, novel agents have been developed to target polyamine metabolism in cancer therapy. These agents, such as ODC inhibitors, showed promise in preclinical and clinical studies, offering potential therapeutic options for patients with cancer [ 22 , 23 ]. However, the role of genes related to PA metabolism in glioma is yet unclear.

Glioma is a broad term encompassing various types of brain tumors originating from glial cells. These cells provide non-neuronal support for the central nervous system. Studies on the metabolic reprogramming of glioma have unveiled the presence of the Warburg effect, altered glucose metabolism, glutamine dependence, changes in lipid metabolism, and mitochondrial dysfunction in the microenvironment of glioma. These findings helped the development of novel treatment strategies targeting specific metabolic pathways and contributed to the design of novel imaging techniques for non-invasive monitoring.

Recent studies on polyamine metabolism reprogramming in glioma have revealed significant advancements [ 24 ]. They found substantial alterations in the synthesis, regulation, and use of polyamines, such as putrescine, spermidine, and spermine, in glioma cells. These metabolic changes play a critical role in glioma progression and have implications for therapeutic strategies [ 25 ]. The identification of specific enzymes and pathways involved in polyamine metabolism in glioma has opened up potential targets for treatment.

Dual targeting of polyamine synthesis and uptake in diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma. Polyamine synthesis is upregulated in diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG), making DIPG susceptible to DFMO [ 26 ]. The co-administration of AMXT 1501 and DFMO showed potent in vitro activity, demonstrating the potential of dual targeting of synthesis and uptake of polyamines as a therapeutic strategy for incurable DIPG.

The study found that polyamines and their urinary and plasma metabolites can be used as diagnostic markers in lung, prostate, colon, pancreatic, and liver cancer [ 27 , 28 ]. Such analyses, combined with precise genomic signatures, may help personalized diagnosis and treatment of cancer based on the use of polyamines as biomarkers. Liu et al. analyzed micro-RNA (miRNA) expression profiles and clinical information from 408 patients with LGGs from the Cancer Genome Atlas in LGGs and identified risk miRNAs for potential prognosis of LGGs [ 29 ]. The SMS gene SGMS1 was associated with this risk score, suggesting that miR-326 might regulate cancer cell growth via the ceramide/SM balance regulated by SMS. Our results showed that genes related to polyamine metabolism were highly expressed in patients with WHO grade IV glioma, and this trend was verified in different databases. Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional risk model identified a significant association between these genes and overall survival in patients with glioma. Furthermore, the LASSO regression machine learning method was used to construct gene prognostic signatures related to polyamine metabolism. Kaplan–Meier analysis revealed poorer survival among patients with higher risk scores in both TCGA and CGGA datasets. In addition, risk scores were associated with different clinical and molecular characteristics in glioma, including WHO grade, IDH status, 1p/19q co-deletion status, and MGMT methylation status.

SMS catalyzes the production of spermine from spermidine and is frequently upregulated in cancers, resulting in elevated polyamine levels required for malignant transformation and tumor progression. SMS has been reported to inhibit apoptosis by reducing ceramide levels in response to various stimuli, including oxidative stress and light damage [ 30 ]. The results of the forest map showed that SMS pairs were important prognostic factors for glioma. In vitro experiments revealed that knockdown of SMS would weaken the activation of the JAK/STAT3 pathway induced by IL-6 and ultimately inhibit the proliferation and invasion abilities of glioma cells. We conducted IHC staining on glioma tissue microarrays to explore the role of SMS in glioma. The results of IHC staining were consistent with the results of bioinformatics analysis. It is worth noting that our results suggest that SMS expression is significantly positively correlated with PD-L1 protein. Further experiments are needed to explore whether SMS participates in regulating the membrane expression of PD-L1.

Recent studies showed that polyamines can regulate the immune system. Honjo et al. found that SPD induces fatty acid oxidation by directly binding to MTP protein, enhancing the function of mitochondria in CD8 + T cells and ultimately affecting the efficacy of PD-1 monoclonal antibody [ 31 ]. De novo synthesis pathway cannot meet the needs of T cell activation. Circulatory polyamines support the proliferation and function of T cells through the compensation pathway. Consistently, genes related to PA metabolism signature were associated with the enrichment of immune-related processes and pathways. Furthermore, genes related to PA metabolism are often associated with Tumor Mutation Burden (TMB). Several studies have confirmed a correlation between TMB levels and the efficacy of immunotherapy [ 32 ], suggesting that an effective PA metabolism risk signature may improve the outcomes of immunotherapy.

Although, more in-depth prospective cohort studies are needed to assess the significance of PA metabolism in glioma. Recently developed metabolomics techniques more comprehensively measure the metabolic profiles of various cancers [ 33 , 34 ]. Such analyses, combined with precise genomic signatures, may help develop more personalized diagnosis and treatment methods for cancer based on polyamines [ 35 ].

Although the findings of this study provide certain clinical guidance for glioma management, several limitations warrant further exploration. The primary constraint lies in the insufficient sample size despite integrating two major glioma databases (TCGA and CGGA), which limits comprehensive analysis of subtle molecular correlations. Notably, the lack of data on geographic distribution and ethnic diversity compromises clinical generalizability. While key protein functions were validated in vitro through scratch assays and Western blotting, systematic in vivo experimental evidence remains absent. Furthermore, the predominant focus on transcriptomic profiling without robust integration of proteomic, epigenetic, and multi-dimensional datasets leaves critical gaps in holistic characterization of glioma heterogeneity. Future investigations should prioritize multi-omics integration strategies to uncover clinically actionable biomarker networks, thereby addressing current limitations in elucidating the pathobiological complexity and therapeutic vulnerabilities of glioma.
sections.conclusion: Polyamine metabolism is a powerful prognostic indicator and can be used as a promising target to strengthen the personalized treatment of glioma.The developed system can improve our understanding of the role of polyamine metabolism in gliomas, paving the way for more precise and effective treatment strategies.
